issues.legal_issue: A fiscal classification imposing higher stamp duty on gratuitous powers of attorney authorizing non-relatives to sell immovable property does not violate equality merely because it is alleged to be arbitrary when the distinction is rationally connected to discouraging indirect property transfers and protecting revenue.
material_facts: The challenged rule imposed stamp duty calculated on the property's market value when an owner, without consideration, authorized an agent outside a specified group of close family members to sell immovable property.
The rule imposed lower duty on comparable powers of attorney given to members of that close family group.
The State explained that the distinction was intended to curb the use of powers of attorney as an indirect means of transferring property and to protect stamp revenue.
The High Court accepted the constitutional challenge, and the State appealed.
issues.conclusion: The classification did not violate Article 14. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, set aside the High Court judgment, and dismissed the writ petitions.
issues.legal_principle: A legislative enactment may be invalidated only for lack of legislative competence or violation of a fundamental or other constitutional provision; it cannot be struck down merely by describing it as arbitrary or unreasonable without identifying a constitutional infirmity. There is a presumption of constitutionality, and an Article 14 classification is permissible when founded on an intelligible differentia rationally related to the statute's object. Legislatures have greater latitude in taxation, and hardship or a court's view of the wisdom or justice of a fiscal measure is not a ground for invalidating it. The Court relied on Article 14 and the Stamp Act, 1899, including Sections 2(10) and 2(21), and on State of A.P. v. McDowell and Co. (1996) 3 SCC 709, Mohd. Hanif Quareshi v. State of Bihar, AIR 1958 SC 731, P. Laxmi Devi (Smt.) v. State of A.P. (2008) 4 SCC 720, R.K. Garg v. Union of India (1981) 4 SCC 675, Karnataka Bank Ltd. v. State of A.P. (2008) 2 SCC 254, and the cited authorities on the presumption of constitutionality and taxation.

rule.if: fiscal_constitutional_challenge and gratuitous_sale_authority and agent_outside_close_family and higher_duty_for_outside_agent and indirect_transfer_and_revenue_purpose

predicates.fiscal_constitutional_challenge: The proceeding challenges the constitutionality of a legislative rule imposing a fiscal charge.
predicates.gratuitous_sale_authority: An owner authorized an agent, without receiving consideration, to sell immovable property.
predicates.agent_outside_close_family: The agent was outside the close family group treated differently by the rule.
predicates.higher_duty_for_outside_agent: The legislative rule imposed a higher duty on authority given to an agent outside that close family group than on authority given to a member of the group.
predicates.indirect_transfer_and_revenue_purpose: The legislature designed the distinction to discourage use of powers of attorney as indirect property transfers and to protect public revenue.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a fiscal rule and an owner gratuitously authorizes an agent outside a favored close family group to sell immovable property, the rule imposes a higher duty on that authority, and the distinction serves the stated purposes of discouraging indirect transfers and protecting revenue, the fiscal classification is constitutionally valid.
